issues.legal_issue: A statutory summary-eviction procedure for municipal premises does not violate equal protection merely because the municipality may use it instead of an ordinary civil suit.
material_facts: The statute allowed the municipal authority to order eviction for specified breaches of occupancy terms or unauthorised occupation, while the municipality could also seek possession through an ordinary civil suit.
The occupants challenged the procedure as giving the municipality unguided discretion to choose between the two remedies.

The authority served a notice stating the grounds for proposed eviction and gave the occupant an opportunity to respond; after the occupant denied unauthorised occupation and did not vacate, the authority ordered him to do so.
The High Court had invalidated the provision, but the Supreme Court had already considered materially identical provisions in earlier decisions.
issues.conclusion: The provision was not invalid under Article 14, and the High Court’s judgment was set aside.
issues.legal_principle: The Court followed Maganlal Chhaganlal (P) Ltd. v. Municipal Corporation of Greater Bombay, which overruled Northern India Caterers Pvt. Ltd. v. State of Punjab, and Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation v. Ramanlal Govindram, which reversed the Gujarat High Court’s ruling on a provision in identical terms. It also relied on State of Gujarat v. Patel Beva Karsan. Those decisions established that the materially identical summary-eviction provision was intra vires; the challenge here therefore failed.

predicates.summary_remedy_choice_challenged: An occupant argued that the authority could choose summary eviction instead of an ordinary civil suit without adequate guiding criteria.
predicates.comparable_supreme_court_decisions_consi: The Supreme Court considered its earlier decisions addressing materially identical statutory eviction procedures.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges the validity of a summary-eviction scheme because the authority can choose that remedy over a civil suit, and the Court considers earlier decisions addressing materially identical procedures, the scheme survives the equal-protection challenge.

issues.legal_issue: A statutory summary-eviction procedure that provides notice and an opportunity to respond does not impose an unreasonable restriction on the then-recognised right to hold property.
material_facts: The statute authorised summary eviction of occupants of municipal premises for specified breaches or unauthorised occupation.

Before making an eviction order, the authority had to give written notice of the grounds and a reasonable opportunity to provide an explanation and evidence; the occupant could also be represented in the proceeding.
The occupant received a notice, responded by denying unauthorised occupation, and was later ordered to vacate.
The High Court had invalidated the provision under Article 19(1)(f), while the Supreme Court had upheld materially identical provisions in earlier decisions.
issues.conclusion: The provision was not invalid under Article 19(1)(f), and the High Court’s judgment was set aside.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied Maganlal Chhaganlal (P) Ltd. v. Municipal Corporation of Greater Bombay, which overruled Northern India Caterers Pvt. Ltd. v. State of Punjab, together with Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation v. Ramanlal Govindram and State of Gujarat v. Patel Beva Karsan. It relied on those decisions’ treatment of materially identical eviction procedures as intra vires, notwithstanding the challenge to the procedure as an unreasonable restriction.
